definition: The term "string grammar" in computational linguistics (and computer languages) refers to the structure of a specific language, such that it can be formatted as a single continuous string of text, without the need to have line-breaks (or newlines) to alter the meaning.
details: The appearance of any text in "column 1" (or any column) of a line does not change the meaning of that text in a string grammar. A string grammar can be used to describe the structure of some natural languages, such as English or French, as well as for some computer languages. Note that the string-based structure is for defining the grammar of a language, rather than the formatting of the language itself. The production rules, of the grammar, are in the form of continuous text strings.

explainer.lead: A string grammar describes the structure of a language as a single continuous string of text, with no reliance on line breaks to carry meaning. It matters where grammars must be expressed as plain text, for natural or computer languages.

tiers.eli5: Like a set of rules written as one long line, where moving a word to a new line wouldn't change what the rules mean.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use string grammars when a language's production rules are written as continuous text, such as parsing or generation specifications. Pitfall: column position or formatting carries no meaning in a string grammar, so any layout-based assumptions are invalid.
tiers.paperLevel: The structure of a language expressible as a single continuous string of text, where production rules take the form of continuous text strings. The text's column position does not change its meaning; the structure describes the grammar, not the formatting of the language itself.

explainer.example: A grammar for a small command language lists its production rules as one continuous string, and indenting or wrapping those rules differently leaves the grammar unchanged.
